title: America Walks Away from Global Democracy
gist: Carnegie's Thomas Carothers documents that the second Trump administration has dismantled eight pillars of fifty years of bipartisan U.S. democracy promotion - cutting democracy aid by close to 90 percent, closing USAID, gutting the NSC and State democracy bureaus, and exiting the UN Human Rights Council, UN Democracy Fund and Open Government Partnership - while adding three actively pro-autocratic practices: open interference in foreign elections (including making a $20 billion Argentina currency swap conditional on a Milei win), veneration of autocrats, and modeling of anti-democratic behavior that leaders from Milei to Orbán to Aliyev have copied. He concludes that for the first time in modern history no major power backs democracy beyond its borders, tilting the global balance pro-autocratic.

insights.claim: The United States has abandoned a fifty-year bipartisan commitment to promoting democracy abroad, reversing or gutting eight distinct pillars of that policy simultaneously — narrative, alliance logic, pressure on backsliders, defense of democracies under attack, support for breakthroughs, institutional capacity, democracy aid, and multilateral backing.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Treat democracy conditionality as removed from the US policy toolkit when pricing political risk in emerging markets — sanctions, aid cutoffs and diplomatic censure over governance no longer follow backsliding.

insights.claim: The 2025 U.S. National Security Strategy contains no reference to supporting democracy abroad and explicitly commits to good relations with other countries without pressing democratic change, making the shift formal doctrine rather than rhetorical drift.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: A codified doctrine is stickier than a mood; assume the policy persists across the administration's tenure rather than reverting with news cycles.
insights.quote: without imposing on them democratic or other social change
insights.locator: 1. Dropping Democracy Support from the Overall Narrative

insights.claim: The one place the 2025 National Security Strategy does engage democracy is Europe, where it frames migration and speech regulation as risking 'civilizational erasure' and expresses optimism about the rise of patriotic European parties — repurposing democracy language as support for the European far right.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Expect continued US political and rhetorical backing for European nationalist parties; this is a live risk premium for EU cohesion and for regulated European tech and media assets.
insights.quote: the growing influence of patriotic European parties
insights.locator: 1. Dropping Democracy Support from the Overall Narrative

insights.claim: Shared democratic values have been explicitly demoted as the foundation of U.S. alliances, with the defense secretary telling an Asian security audience in May 2026 that durable partnerships do not rest on idealistic values.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Allied trust is now transactional and renegotiable; hedge for allies diversifying defense procurement and security arrangements away from Washington.
insights.quote: the bedrock of a durable partnership is not based on idealistic values

insights.claim: A 2025 State Department directive instructs staff to avoid commenting on the fairness, integrity or legitimacy of foreign electoral processes, removing the single most routine instrument of U.S. pressure on backsliding leaders.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Election manipulation in partner states now carries near-zero US diplomatic cost — a structurally lower bar for incumbents to entrench, and for the political risk that follows.
insights.quote: should avoid opining on the fairness or integrity of an electoral process, its legitimacy, or the democratic values of the country in question
insights.locator: 3. Not Criticizing or Pressuring Democratic Backsliders

insights.claim: U.S. democracy aid was cut by close to 90 percent within six months of the second Trump term, principally by closing USAID and dismantling the State Department's democracy bureau.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: A near-total funding stop for election monitoring, rule-of-law and independent-media programs worldwide; expect measurable degradation in governance indicators used by EM risk models.

insights.claim: In fiscal 2024 Congress directed $2.9 billion to USAID and State Department democracy aid plus $315 million to the National Endowment for Democracy, which is why the elimination of USAID and most State programs amounts to roughly a 90 percent reduction.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: The concrete size of the vacuum — roughly $2.9bn a year — is the number other donors would have to replace, and they cannot.

insights.claim: The National Endowment for Democracy survived repeated administration attempts to zero out its budget thanks to congressional support, but it represents only around 10 percent of pre-2025 U.S. democracy aid.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Congress is the only remaining brake on this line of spending; NED's survival is symbolic rather than a material offset.

insights.claim: The cuts to democracy aid were a deliberate target rather than collateral damage from the broader aid demolition, driven by a view that such aid was a cover for 'woke' values and hostile to friendly right-leaning governments.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Ideological targeting means the cuts are unlikely to be quietly restored through appropriations workarounds; plan for a durable absence.

insights.claim: European governments trying to backfill lost U.S. democracy assistance are overwhelmed: the amount of aid lost exponentially exceeds their capacity to compensate.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Do not model European donors as a substitute; the net global funding level for civil society and independent media steps down, not sideways.

insights.claim: A 2025 executive order mandated elimination of the U.S. Agency for Global Media alongside a sustained effort to shut Voice of America, removing a broadcasting channel that projected democratic values abroad for decades.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: State-aligned broadcasters from Russia and China face one less competitor in contested information markets.

insights.claim: The three institutional legs of U.S. democracy policymaking have been removed or crippled: the NSC directorate on democracy and human rights was eliminated, the State Department's Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor was heavily cut, and USAID's Bureau for Democracy, Human Rights, and Governance was disbanded.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
entities: Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor
insights.so_what: Even a future administration that wants to rebuild democracy policy would face years of capacity reconstruction — the reversal is not a switch that can be flipped.
insights.locator: 6. Shrinking U.S. Institutional Capacity on Democracy

insights.claim: The administration has withdrawn from the UN Human Rights Council, the Universal Periodic Review, the UN Democracy Fund the United States co-founded with India in 2005, the International Institute for Justice and the Rule of Law, the Open Government Partnership the United States helped found in 2011, and International IDEA, while cutting its contribution to the UN Development Programme.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
entities: International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance
insights.so_what: Multilateral governance bodies lose their largest funder and convener simultaneously — watch for budget-driven contraction and for China and other states filling the institutional space.
insights.locator: 8. Not Backing International and Regional Organizations

insights.claim: Washington has demanded that the OSCE curtail election monitoring in member states, proposed zeroing out its contribution to the Organization of American States, and pushed the OAS away from democracy building — attacking regional election-observation infrastructure directly.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Credible third-party election observation is the main external check on manipulated votes; its degradation raises contested-election risk in Europe and Latin America.
insights.locator: 8. Not Backing International and Regional Organizations

insights.claim: U.S. policy toward the African Union now explicitly disclaims interest in lecturing on democratic norms and elevates commercial diplomacy as the top priority, making resource and trade access the organizing principle of Africa policy.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Africa engagement is now framed as deal flow, not governance — relevant for mining, energy and infrastructure exposure across the continent.
insights.quote: making commercial diplomacy a top priority
insights.locator: 8. Not Backing International and Regional Organizations

insights.claim: Rather than regulate digital surveillance technology, the administration has deployed it through ICE and other agencies, emulating the digital repression tactics of autocratic regimes like China, while attacking the EU's Digital Services Act that underpins information integrity in Europe.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Domestic surveillance-tech demand is a policy tailwind while transatlantic tech regulation becomes a live diplomatic battleground for platform companies.

insights.claim: The administration has reversed ten to fifteen years of U.S. leadership on international anti-corruption, and because corruption in democracies alienates citizens and opens the door to anti-democratic populists — as Brazil's scandals did for Bolsonaro in 2018 — the reversal has second-order democratic costs at home and abroad.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Lower enforcement risk for cross-border bribery near term, but higher political instability risk in high-corruption markets over a multi-year horizon.

insights.claim: Cutting development aid removes one of the main economic carrots the United States used to reward democratic reformers, so the loss is not just humanitarian but eliminates Washington's principal non-coercive lever over governance.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: With carrots gone, the remaining US instruments are tariffs and sanctions — expect a more coercive, more volatile toolkit in US-emerging-market relations.

insights.claim: Support for Ukraine has been reduced across every channel simultaneously: paused military aid and intelligence sharing, no new military aid, terminated or cut non-military aid for health, infrastructure and education, and no diplomatic advocacy in international forums.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Ukraine's external funding floor is now European, not American — a persistent fiscal drag on EU budgets and a driver of European defense spending.

insights.claim: The administration has made no effort to increase economic sanctions on Russia except once in October 2025, while pausing or weakening existing measures — meaning sanctions pressure on Moscow has net decayed rather than escalated.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Sanctions relief optionality on Russian assets and energy is structurally higher than consensus assumed; the escalation path has effectively been switched off.

insights.claim: Trump signaled in July 2026 that he would license Ukraine to build Patriot missiles domestically, then reversed within the same month — a template showing pro-Ukraine policy signals should be discounted until implemented.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Fade headline-driven moves in European defense and Ukraine-reconstruction names on announcement; wait for execution.

insights.claim: Trump's 2026 pivot from hawkishness on China to seeking cooperation with Beijing, including an apparent willingness to negotiate with Beijing over a planned $14 billion weapons package for Taiwan, has raised questions about the firmness of the U.S. security commitment to Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Taiwan arms sales are now a bargaining chip in US-China talks — a tail risk for the semiconductor supply chain and for defense exporters booking Taiwan orders.

insights.claim: The administration punished Brazil with high tariffs in response to Bolsonaro's conviction for coup-plotting, using trade policy to defend an anti-democratic ally rather than to advance U.S. economic interest.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Tariff risk in this administration can be triggered by a partner's domestic judicial or political decisions, not just trade balances — widen the scenario set for country trade exposure.

insights.claim: Post-breakthrough governments in Bangladesh, Nepal and Syria are receiving far less U.S. aid at precisely the moment of maximum fragility, and Hungary's new post-Orbán government seeking to rebuild democracy has received no U.S. diplomatic or economic support.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Transition states lose the external cash cushion that historically smoothed reform; higher probability of relapse, currency stress and IMF dependence in these markets.

insights.claim: Trump has openly endorsed candidates in foreign elections including Nasry Asfura in Honduras (November 2025), Takaichi Sanae in Japan (February 2026), Orbán in Hungary (April 2026) and Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia (June 2026), typically via Truth Social.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: US endorsement is now a recurring, schedulable event risk around elections in Europe, Latin America and Asia — price it into pre-election FX and local-rate volatility.

insights.claim: Shortly before Argentina's October 2025 legislative elections Trump made a promised $20 billion currency swap explicitly conditional on the vote favoring Javier Milei, directly linking U.S. financial support to an electoral outcome.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: The clearest case of US balance-sheet support being priced to an election result — a precedent that makes sovereign support lines politically contingent and therefore less reliable collateral.

insights.claim: The administration used non-financial levers too, granting Karol Nawrocki a White House visit before Poland's May 2025 runoff and sending Vance to Budapest the week before Hungary's April 2026 vote to urge Hungarians to back Orbán to stand for Western civilization.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Access to the White House is itself a campaign asset in pro-American electorates; track which candidates get it as a leading indicator of US-aligned policy after elections.

insights.claim: Interference is concentrated in Europe and Latin America because those politics run along a clear left-right axis, unlike many African, Asian and Middle Eastern systems — a targeting logic that predicts where the next interventions will land.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Use the left-right-axis filter to anticipate which upcoming elections carry US-intervention risk.

insights.claim: The deeper damage from open U.S. election interference is normative rather than case-by-case: it dissolves the global norm against external meddling and places the United States on the same plane as Russia and other autocratic powers that have been escalating interference.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Expect more, not less, cross-border election meddling globally as the reputational cost collapses — a rising structural source of political-risk surprises.

themes.theme: Autocrat Veneration and the Modeling Channel

insights.claim: Trump's praise of autocrats differs qualitatively from past presidents' pragmatic flattery: where predecessors praised undemocratic leaders for specific strategic or economic benefits, Trump repeatedly admires their methods of ruling and their strength, making it their autocratic nature that attracts him.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: This is a norm signal, not a transaction — it lowers the perceived cost of autocratic consolidation worldwide and sustains the political-risk regime regardless of individual deals.

insights.claim: At the July 2026 NATO summit in Ankara, Trump criticized democratic allies while singling out for praise only Erdoğan, Netanyahu and Xi — a public ranking that inverts the traditional alliance hierarchy.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Alliance cohesion discounts belong in European defense and sovereign risk assumptions; NATO's political guarantee is weaker than its treaty text.

insights.claim: The modeling effect is documented across multiple countries: Milei's escalating attacks on journalists in Argentina, Vučić's intensified assault on Serbian independent media after U.S. media assistance ended, Netanyahu's renewed judicial overhaul once Biden's opposition disappeared, Orbán's antifa terrorist designation and USAID-justified civil society crackdown, and Aliyev's shuttering of aid and development groups in Azerbaijan.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Domestic institutional erosion is now correlated across many markets at once, which means governance-driven risk repricing can come in waves rather than idiosyncratically.
insights.quote: emboldened by Donald Trump's toxic rhetoric

insights.claim: Foreign leaders have copied specific U.S. tactics rather than just the mood, with Orbán adopting the antifa terrorist designation and using the U.S. demonization of USAID to justify defunding Hungarian civil society groups he accused of trying to topple his government.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Tactic diffusion is traceable and predictable — when a new US tactic appears, expect replication in MAGA-aligned governments within months.

insights.claim: Trump's own musings about a third term plausibly contributed to Bukele and his allies amending El Salvador's constitution to eliminate term limits, and the administration's response to that autocratizing step was neutral or even positive.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Term-limit removal is spreading with US acquiescence; extend political-continuity assumptions in affected markets but raise the eventual rupture risk.

themes.theme: The Pro-Democracy Case and Its Limits

insights.claim: Venezuela is the administration's strongest claim to pro-democracy action but is ambiguous: Maduro was removed, yet the new equilibrium around Delcy Rodríguez is softened autocracy with some economic reform, opposition leader Maria Corina Machado has been sidelined, and it is unclear the administration wants more than access to Venezuelan oil.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Venezuela reopening is an oil-access trade with a politically fragile counterparty, not a democratization story — size positions to the durability of a personalist arrangement.

insights.claim: The U.S. blockade on oil supplies to Cuba is creating severe economic pressure and Trump has spoken of taking Cuba, but the likely landing zone may be limited political change paired with an opening to U.S. business, mirroring the Venezuela pattern.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: A Cuba opening would most likely be a commercial access deal rather than a democratic transition — position for first-mover business access, not institutional reform.
insights.quote: I do believe I'll be . . . having the honor of taking Cuba.

insights.claim: Trump's February 2026 call for Iranians to take over their government during U.S. military action was unplanned, ran into a rally-around-the-flag effect and a population depleted by the massacre of thousands of protesters two months earlier, and was abandoned in favor of negotiating over the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's nuclear program.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: US Iran policy has converged on a transactional accord covering Hormuz transit and nuclear limits — the relevant variable for oil risk premia, not regime change.

insights.claim: The administration's self-described democracy defense in Europe — punishing governments over speech regulation and the exclusion of far-right parties from coalitions — is read by the targeted European governments as interference in their sovereign policy choices, not as democracy support.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Transatlantic friction now runs through domestic European political arrangements, a broader and less negotiable conflict surface than trade disputes.

insights.claim: For the first time in modern history none of the top international powers is committed to supporting democracy beyond its borders, so the overall balance of global geostrategic power now leans distinctly pro-autocratic.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: This is the regime-level claim: assume a structurally higher baseline of authoritarian consolidation, contested elections and arbitrary policy risk across the investable world.
insights.quote: none of the top international powers is committed to supporting democracy beyond its borders

insights.claim: Domestic agency still dominates outcomes: Hungary's citizens chose a pro-democratic path in 2026 even though the United States, Russia and China all favored continued Orbán rule, showing external pressure is not determinative.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Do not treat the US retreat as deterministic for any single country; domestic political cycles can still produce sharp, tradeable regime turnarounds.

insights.claim: Pro-democratic turnarounds have actually been increasing in recent years even amid a twenty-year global democratic recession, usually driven by citizens demanding a genuine political voice — so the trend is contested rather than one-directional.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Two-sided distribution: budget for upside regime surprises in stressed autocracies as well as downside erosion in current democracies.

insights.claim: The magnitude of the eventual damage depends primarily on duration: if the new U.S. stance proves long-term it becomes a serious drag on democracy globally, while a short-lived version does less though still real damage.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: The key variable to track is the 2028 US electoral cycle and whether the policy architecture survives it — that is the switch on the whole thesis.
